state.case_summary:
A 49-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a 5-day history of intermittent throbbing abdominal pain that began periumbilically and localized to the right lower quadrant, associated with nausea and increased stool frequency. Her medical history was notable for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in 2009 and a supracervical hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy for uterine fibroids in 2012, at which time endometriosis was noted. Examination showed moderate tenderness in the right lower quadrant and a positive Rovsing sign. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed lobulated tubular soft tissue and inflammation adjacent to the terminal ileum/ileocecal valve, and the appendix was not identified, leading to a presumptive diagnosis of acute appendicitis. The patient received broad-spectrum antibiotics and underwent diagnostic laparoscopy, which showed mild inflammatory changes of the terminal ileum and adhesions but no appendix despite full mobilization of the cecum and small-bowel run; biopsy of inflamed areas demonstrated acute inflammation and foci of endometriosis. The patient improved and was discharged but returned two hours later with sharp right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Repeat white-cell count was 13.2×10^9/L. Repeat CT showed small-bowel obstruction at the terminal ileum, likely secondary to an adjacent pericecal soft-tissue mass. The differential diagnosis included inverted appendix versus neoplasm.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. appendiceal intussusception
B. the mass was inverted appendix versus neoplasm
C. Acute appendicitis was initially favored
D. Crohn’s disease was considered but ruled out intraoperatively
E. Neoplasm was included in the differential of the pericecal mass
F. Inverted appendix (appendiceal intussusception) was also considered for the pericecal mass
G. None
H. None
